newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Westendorp runs afoul of U.S. diplomacy in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Westendorp runs afoul of U.S. diplomacy in Bosnia.

text.p: The new international envoy to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, may well be longing for quarrels in the European Union instead of the vicious political climate he has encountered in the Balkans.
Less than two months after taking over as the High Representative to Bosnia, Westendorp has collided with the United States government, which dominates peacemaking efforts in former Yugoslavia.

A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, slammed Westendorp on Monday, accusing him spending too much time outside Bosnia and of mismanaging a dispute over the distribution of ambassadorial posts.
Westendorp "has not spent nearly as much time in Bosnia as we had hoped," said the official.

The 60-year old Spanish diplomat, who served as foreign minister and envoy to the United Nations, came under criticism after he departed this week for his second holiday since he arrived in Sarajevo in mid-June.
Diplomats said State Department officials were angry with the High Representive's office for taking the lead in negotiations between rival Bosnia leaders over the distribution of diplomatic posts.

The U.S. embassy in Sarajevo said on Tuesday that Washington supported Westendorp but that it was "concerned that there must be adequate leadership and consultation on the part of the High Representative and his office".
Like Carl Bildt, his Swedish predecessor, Westendorp finds himself squeezed between European countries and Washington over how to enforce the peace treaty agreed in Dayton, Ohio in 1995.
The United States, which brokered the peace accords, dominates diplomacy in Bosnia, the NATO-led peace force and the monitoring of post-war elections.
Over the past 18 months, U.S. officials sometimes pushed aside Bildt when he and European powers disagreed with Washington's approach.
Westendorp's aides said the American broadside was "outrageous" and "inaccurate". They said the U.S. embassy was informed throughout negotiations on the dispute over diplomatic posts.
"We have nothing to apologise for," said one aide.
The American criticism of Westendorp came shortly before a visit to Bosnia by U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, the architect of the peace treaty.
Some of Westendorp's aides said U.S. officials might be trying to denigrate the High Representative's office to lay the ground for a "breakthrough" during Holbrooke's trip.
Westendorp is a charismatic, career diplomat who played an important role in the European Union's Maastricht treaty negotiations.
But the subtle negotiating techniques he learned in the halls of the EU or the U.N. do not necessarily translate to the rough world of Balkan machinations.
Since arriving six weeks ago, Westendorp has made only rare appearances before the press and stumbled occasionally on the complicated terms set out in the Dayton accords.
His office had to explain away his apparently incorrect reference to a Monday deadline for reaching agreement on a citizenship law.
His advisers say he is still at the beginning of his assignment and has spent time outside Bosnia as part of vital talks with diplomats in Russia and the European Union.
Although he may not deserve the credit, there have been two major successes for the peace process during Westendorp's tenure.
The central multi-ethnic parliament adopted important economic legislation in June and NATO troops launched a ground-breaking arrest operation against two Serbs indicted for war crimes last month.
